newsitem.title: JAPAN: IAEA to closely monitor Japan nuclear programme.
newsitem.headline: IAEA to closely monitor Japan nuclear programme.

text.p: The International Atomic Energy Agency will be keeping a close watch on Japan's troubled nuclear power programme, a spokesman for the global watchdog said Thursday.

"The turmoil created in Japan is being monitored closely by the IAEA and by the entire nuclear community," IAEA spokesman David Kyd told Reuters in a telephone interview from the agency's headquarters in Vienna.

Kyd's comment followed Wednesday's meeting in Tokyo between IAEA Director-General Hans Blix and Toshiyuki Kondo, president of Japan's state-run nuclear power firm, Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC).
During the 40-minute meeting, Kondo spelled out to Blix the circumstances surrounding Japan's worst ever nuclear accident, nuclear agency officials said.

Talks between the IAEA chief and Kondo, also attended by PNC vice president Kunihiko Uematsu, followed comments by Blix earlier in the day urging honest and immediate disclosure of nuclear accidents or shutdowns in Japan.

"The public demands stronger safety in the nuclear (than in other industries) and we have to respond to that," Blix said in an interview with the Japan Times newspaper on Wednesday. In March, a fire and an explosion at the Tokaimura processing plant 120 km (75 miles) north of Tokyo exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation in the country's worst atomic incident.
After the accident, it was discovered that the chief investigator of Japan's top nuclear agency destroyed photographs of the fire in a botched cover-up attempt.

It was also revealed that cleaners at the facility first removed, and then replaced, debris caused by the accident. The scandal struck a killer blow to PNC's public image, already in severe meltdown from past gaffes.

"It is perfectly clear to us that the technologies involved are highly complex, and accidents will happen, but this incident has sent ripples across the entire international energy community," Kyd said.

"The Japanese approach to crisis management is clearly different to those seen in the United States and Europe," he added. Official explanations on the Tokaimura accident have so far been murky, the latest being an April statement by the Science and Technology Agency indicating the fire may possibly have been triggered by a change in the chemical mix used for the reprocessing nuclear waste at the facility.

Since December 1995, when Monju, Japan's showcase fast-breeder reactor on the Sea of Japan coast, leaked an estimated two to three tonnes of liquid sodium from a cooling system, a long list of additional accidents and cover-ups have placed PNC and Japan's ambitious nuclear energy plans under growing public scrutiny.
There are calls for energy-starved Japan to review its plans to expand its reliance on nuclear power from the current 33 percent to 42 percent by 2010.
